title: Replacing Russian Barrels Will Hike Costs for Indian Refiners, Industry Warns
excerpt: With Trump having signed the Russia sanctions law authorising up to 100% tariffs on top buyers of Russian oil, India's refiners face costlier spot cargoes, freight and insurance - just as Russian crude hit a record 55% share of imports.
body:
• With Trump having signed the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act — authorising tariffs of up to 100% on top buyers of Russian oil — India faces the prospect of replacing discounted Russian barrels at the worst possible moment.
  • A refining executive told the Times of India that buying from Africa, Latin America and the US instead would mean "higher spot prices and increased freight and insurance premiums," with alternative routes squeezed by Hormuz and Bab el-Mandeb disruptions.
  • India's Russian crude share hit a record ~55% in July (Kpler data); the tariffs are discretionary, not automatic, but refiners like Reliance, MRPL and HPCL-Mittal are already expected to wind down Russian purchases.

The law is signed; the arithmetic is now the story. Days after President Donald Trump signed the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026 — giving him authority to impose tariffs of up to 100% on the five largest buyers of Russian crude — Indian refiners are confronting what it would actually cost to walk away from Russian barrels. The answer, according to the industry, is not cheap.

A senior executive at an oil refining company told the Times of India that replacing Russian barrels under current geopolitics would mean increasing "imports from Africa, Latin America and US," adding that "buying from geographies spread afield will add to costs due to higher spot prices and increased freight and insurance premiums." India already imports crude from nearly 40 countries; the issue is not availability, it is price.

Record dependence, bad timing

India's exposure has never been larger. Kpler vessel-tracking data put July imports from Russia at roughly 2.8 million barrels a day — about 55.5% of India's total imports of around 5 million bpd. August already cooled to 2.08 mbpd, or 45%, as U.S. sanctions on Russian majors Rosneft and Lukoil — effective November 21 — began biting. Reliance Industries, MRPL and HPCL-Mittal Energy are expected to suspend Russian purchases.

The cruel part is the timing. The alternative supply routes are the ones under strain: Strait of Hormuz and Bab el-Mandeb shipping is disrupted amid the Iran war, and a drone attack damaged Saudi Arabia's East-West pipeline last week, the Times of India reported. So a tariff-driven pivot would land on refiners' margins through costlier spot cargoes, longer voyages and fatter insurance premiums — at the exact moment India is most dependent on discounted barrels.

What the law actually does

Precision matters here, because some early reporting blurred it. The law authorises — but does not require — the president to impose tariffs of up to 100% on goods from the five largest purchasers of Russian crude oil or natural gas, identified by the USTR in consultation with the Secretaries of State and Energy, with the list reviewed every 180 days. It also provides for tariffs of up to 500% on goods imported directly from Russia. No country is named; imposing the tariffs, and at what rate up to the ceiling, is at the president's discretion, with waiver authority on national security grounds.

India has said it will continue buying oil "through diversified sourcing."

"This issue has been discussed at high levels in recent months with various US interlocutors. Its potential implications for not just the bilateral relationship but also the international energy market have been very clearly articulated by Indian side."

— India's foreign ministry, quoted in the Times of India

How India got here

India became the top buyer of discounted Russian crude after the 2022 Ukraine invasion, rising from about 100,000 bpd (roughly 2.5%) in 2021 to around 1.8 mbpd (39%) in 2023 and the July 2026 record. There is precedent for forced pivots: Iran supplied about 12% of India's imports until March 2019, when U.S. sanctions halted purchases, and Venezuelan oil's share fell from over 6% to zero in 2020–21. Each rerouting carried a cost.

What it means for the diaspora

Tariffs of up to 100% on Indian goods would raise prices on Indian exports to the U.S. and feed energy-inflation concerns on both sides of the Pacific. The discretionary nature of the law cuts both ways: it gives diplomacy room, but leaves every refiner and exporter pricing in uncertainty.

What's next

Watch the USTR's buyer list and the 180-day review cycle — and the waiver decision. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has urged the law be implemented "fully and as quickly as possible." For India, the near-term tells are simpler: August's import data showed the Russian share already falling; the question is whether the pivot to African, Latin American and U.S. barrels shows up in refiners' margins before it shows up in diplomacy.
image_caption: Indian refiners warn costs will rise as they replace discounted Russian barrels with alternative crude supplies.
